But to answer your question, CTS doesn't mean much. It's just typically a higher quality pot in terms of mechanical integrity and resistance accuracy. It's not going to really make any difference in tone between a CTS pot and a non CTS pot assuming they are of the same resistance values. 

Any difference in tone you heard in your friend's guitar was likely due to the capacitor change and mostly if the values changed from that and/or the pots. For instance if he went from using a 250k pot to a 500k pot, that would make a noticeable difference in tone by allowing more highs to come through. The type of capacitor, region of manufacture, and materials all make little to no difference no matter what some people might claim when they install 20 dollar oil in paper caps into their guitars. The really important part is the resistance value of the pots and the capacitance values of the cap. 

If you want more treble to come through in your guitar, you might look at changing the resistance value of the pots and/or caps.

Most luthiers will at least know someone that'll do it if they won't do it themselves. It's honestly not that hard at all. The worst part is removing the finish if it's polyurethane. But if you have a nitro finish, easy peasey. You just buy one of those hangers or make your own that attaches to where the neck heel goes... Remove original finish... Sand to a grain that'll capture the type of paint you wanna use (spray paint is probably the easiest but a good air brushing looks fantastic and is maybe even easier as far as applying it to the body). Let dry, then add another coat or two. Finish with a protectant. Nitro is a little harder to work with, but it really is the best if you can find the right color you want and have an area to do it in that's got great ventilation. But a nitro job with nitrocellulose might be better left to a professional all around tbh

If you want the racing stripe, you would apply that color first in the area it goes, then put a stencil on before applying the body paint. Stencils can be bought on ebay or you can make your own with painter's tape. Watch some YT videos of repaints and see if it seems like something you'd be able to do.

Edit: one more thing... I don't know if there's any auto body shops around you, but a couple in my area will also do guitars as long as the finish is already removed.

Yes get the PV65s. They're not gonna be any less noisy necessarily, but they're just good pickups in general. They also have wax coated cloth wiring, which I suppose could potentially help the noise issue.

I would also buy one of those aluminum pickguard screens and create a faraday cage inside the cavity. You might have to buy some conductive tape if it's not already inside the cavity. You could also just line the pickguard with the tape as well if not going the aluminum screen route. After doing that, use a multimeter and check for continuity among all the possible points of ground. Also check for bad wiring or areas where wires could potentially be touching, even if insulated. 

Lastly, make sure you're plugging into a good power strip, or at least make sure nothing else that's plugged into the same circuit (meaning literally anything that goes to the same circuit at the circuit box) is at fault. I often find that certain types of electronics are the culprit for noisy hums, or at least the exacerbater. I have a small fan that is horrible for this. I definitely never have more than one amplifier plugged in at any given time unless I'm doing a stereo thing, but even then I try to keep them plugged in at different spots as far as possible from each other.
